Here are two polished versions of the text. Because the original is a famous Scots dialect poem by Robert Burns, it has been rendered below in both **Eloquent Literary Prose** (ideal for standard readability) and **Polished Modern Verse** (maintaining the original poetic structure).

---

### Option 1: Eloquent Literary Prose
> My heart is breaking, my dear sister, and I earnestly seek your counsel. While it grieves me to anger my family, I am at a loss as to what to do regarding Tam Glen. I am convinced that with such a fine gentleman, I could happily endure a life of humble means. Indeed, what care I for wallowing in wealth if I am forbidden from marrying Tam Glen?
>
> Consider Lowrie, the Laird of Dumeller—that brute strides into the house with his pompous greetings, boasting endlessly of his fortune. Yet for all his money, when could he ever dance with the grace of Tam Glen? My mother constantly plagues me with warnings against young men, insisting they flatter only to deceive; yet who could ever suspect Tam Glen of such falsehood? My father promises me a handsome fortune of ten hundred marks if I agree to renounce him. Yet if fate has ordained that I must marry, who else could my heart possibly choose?
>
> Even the omens point to him. Last night during the Valentine's drawing, my heart leaped to my throat when I drew a name three times in succession—and every single time, it bore the name "Tam Glen." Furthermore, last Halloween, as I observed the ritual of drying my wet sleeve, his very apparition walked into the house, right down to Tam Glen's distinct gray trousers!
>
> Please do not delay in giving me your advice. I will gladly give you my prized black hen if you will simply counsel me to marry the young man I love so dearly: Tam Glen.

---

### Option 2: Polished Modern Verse
> My heart is breaking, dear sister; pray lend me your counsel today.  
> It grieves me to anger my family, yet what other path can I weigh?  
> With so fine a gentleman by me, in poverty I could manage fine:  
> What care I for riches and fortune, if Tam Glen can never be mine?  
>
> There is Lowrie, the Laird of Dumeller—a brute as he enters the door!  
> He brags and he boasts of his money, yet grace he has none on the floor.  
> My mother persistently warns me that young men flatter to feign,  
> Yet who could suspect such deceit in a lover as true as Tam Glen?  
>
> My father vows ten hundred marks if I choose to forsake him for good,  
> Yet if destiny calls me to marry, no other could stand where he stood.  
> Last night at the drawing of names, my heart gave a terrible bound,  
> For thrice I drew out a ticket, and thrice was Tam’s name to be found!  
>
> And last Halloween as I waited, my wet sleeve hung up by the door,  
> His likeness walked into the dwelling, in the gray trousers Tam always wore!  
> So give me your counsel, dear sister, and do not delay or refrain;  
> I’ll give you my finest black hen if you tell me to marry Tam Glen.

Dearest sister, my heart is breaking, so please offer me your guidance without delay. Upsetting my entire family breaks my heart, yet I am at a loss regarding what to do about my feelings for Tam Glen. I am convinced that partnering with such a fine young man would allow us to survive even severe poverty. After all, what good is living in luxury if I am forbidden from becoming Tam Glen's wife? 

Consider Lowrie, the landowner of Dumeller—what a rude beast he is when he struts into our home shouting greetings! He constantly boasts about his immense wealth, yet he completely lacks the grace and dancing skills that Tam Glen possesses. 

Furthermore, my mother endlessly bombards me with warnings against young suitors, claiming their compliments are mere tactics to trick me. But who could ever accuse Tam Glen of such deceit? My father even offered me a bribe of one thousand marks if I agree to abandon him. Yet, if destiny has decreed that I am meant to be with him, then Tam Glen is surely the only husband meant for me.

Signs of fate have proven this to be true. Just yesterday evening, as we drew names for Valentine's Day, my heart leaped into my throat because I picked the exact same name three times in a row, and each slip bore the name "Tam Glen." Furthermore, as you recall, during the previous Halloween, I remained awake performing the ritual with my soaked shirt sleeve. Sure enough, an apparition walked into the room possessing his exact appearance, right down to Tam Glen's signature gray trousers!

Therefore, my dear sister, do not hesitate to give me your counsel. I will gladly reward you with my beautiful black hen if you simply instruct me to wed the young man I cherish so deeply: Tam Glen.

This conviction is put to the test by the presence of Lowrie, a wealthy suitor pursuing her hand. Though Lowrie offers the financial security her family craves, the speaker finds him insufferable. She views him as boastful, arrogant, and fundamentally inferior to Tam Glen in every quality that truly matters. Where others see Lowrie’s fortune as an enviable prize, she sees only a pompous man whose riches cannot purchase her affection or respect.

Her unwavering devotion to Tam, however, puts her at direct odds with her parents. Her mother, cynical and protective, warns her that men are inherently deceitful and that romantic promises are easily broken. Her father takes a more pragmatic approach, attempting to sway her by offering a substantial financial bribe if she agrees to give Tam up forever. Yet, despite her mother’s bitter warnings and her father’s monetary temptation, the speaker’s devotion remains unshaken.

Reinforcing her emotional certainty is a deep-seated belief that her union with Tam is ordained by fate itself. She recalls how a series of romantic omens on key folk holidays have consistently pointed toward him. From mystical signs observed during Halloween rituals to the traditional auguries of Valentine’s Day, every superstition and natural token has confirmed that Tam Glen is her destined partner. To turn away from him, she feels, would be to defy destiny.

Ultimately, the speaker seeks validation from the one person she trusts to understand her plight. In a gesture that is both whimsical and deeply sincere, she offers her sister her most prized possession—her valued black hen—as a reward if only her sister will give her the advice she longs to hear: to follow her heart, brave her parents' disapproval, and marry Tam Glen.

The heavy oak door of the cottage had barely closed, but the echoes of her parents' harsh demands still lingered in the quiet room. 

Jean sat on the edge of her wooden chest, her hands trembling in her lap. For weeks, her mother and father had waged a persistent war against her heart. They spoke constantly of land, of cattle, and of the comfortable life offered by the wealthy, older suitor who had recently asked for her hand. He promised a warm hearth, fine woollen shawls, and a cupboard that would never run bare. But to Jean, his presence was as cold as a winter frost. Her heart belonged entirely to Tam Glen—a young man whose pockets were empty of gold, but whose spirit was rich with kindness, laughter, and an unyielding devotion to her.

"A girl cannot eat moonlight, nor can she clothe herself in sweet words," her mother had chided that very evening, setting down a pewter plate with unnecessary force. "Tam Glen has nothing to his name but a pair of patched boots and a song. You will marry where there is substance, Jean, and that is an end to it."

Overwhelmed and suffocating under the weight of her family’s expectations, Jean slipped out of her room and stole down the narrow hallway to her sister Lizzie’s bedchamber. Lizzie was her truest confidante, the one person who understood that a life without love was merely a slow kind of dying.

"They mean to break my spirit, Lizzie," Jean whispered, sinking onto the side of her sister's bed as tears threatened to spill. "They would sell me to the highest bidder and call it love."

Lizzie sat up, wrapping a thick quilt around her sister’s shoulders. "Mother and Father look at the world through the lens of hardship," Lizzie said gently. "They fear poverty. But tell me, Jean—what does your own soul say?"

"My soul speaks only Tam’s name," Jean replied softly. "Yet, when they yell so loudly, I begin to fear my own judgment. So... I asked the old ways for an answer. I turned to the omens."

Lizzie listened intently as Jean revealed the secret rituals she had performed over the past several nights, desperate for a sign from fate to guide her through the storm.

"On All Hallows' Eve," Jean began, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, "I went alone into the dark garden and pulled a kale stalk from the earth, just as the old wives teach. I closed my eyes and drew it up—it came forth straight, strong, and sweet to the tongue, with rich earth clinging to its roots. It was the very image of an honest, steadfast husband. And when I checked the name of the spirit attached to it, everything pointed to Tam."

Lizzie smiled faintly, but Jean continued, her expression earnest.

"I thought perhaps it was mere chance," Jean admitted. "So, the following night, I took a red apple and peeled it in one long, unbroken ribbon, asking the heavens to reveal the initials of the man I am destined to wed. I threw the skin over my left shoulder, and when it landed upon the floorboard, it had curled into the distinct shape of a 'T' and a 'G'."

"And still you doubted?" Lizzie asked softly.

"I was terrified of my own hope," Jean confessed. "So tonight, before the sun went down, I tried the final trial. I took a skein of blue yarn and tossed it into the dark opening of the old kiln, holding fast to the end of the thread. I wound it back, calling out into the shadows, *'Who holds the end of my line?'* And Lizzie... a voice echoed back from the dark, clear as a bell, speaking his name."

Lizzie reached out and took Jean’s trembling hands in her own. "The signs are not confusing, sister. You did not just ask the shadows; you asked the universe, and it has answered you three times over. The omens do not lie, but more importantly, neither does your heart."

Jean looked into her sister’s reassuring eyes, feeling the heavy knot of dread in her chest begin to unravel. The pressure from her parents had made her feel isolated and powerless, but the quiet certainty of the folk traditions—combined with Lizzie’s steady support—reignited her courage. 

Her parents saw wealth as a shield against the world, but Jean realized that a life built solely on material riches would be an empty shell. Tam Glen offered a partnership forged in genuine affection, a bond that fate itself had repeatedly affirmed. No amount of land, gold, or parental disapproval could alter what was written in the stars.

"I will not marry for money," Jean said, her voice growing firm for the first time in weeks. "Let them keep their lands and their grand promises. Tomorrow, I will tell Father that my choice is made."

"And Tam?" Lizzie asked, a warm smile spreading across her face.

Jean stood up, smoothing her apron, a newfound peace washing over her. "Tam and I have destiny on our side. We may start with nothing, but we will have everything that truly matters."

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you give me a classic Scottish poem written in traditional dialect about a young woman torn between rich suitors and her true love?
counterfactuals.output:
The quintessential poem for this theme is **"Tam Glen,"** written in 1790 by Scotland’s national bard, **Robert Burns**. 

In this classic poem, a young woman named Meg confides in her friend ("tittie") about the immense pressure from her family to marry one of several wealthy suitors (like the landowners Lowrie or Sandy). Despite their riches, her heart belongs entirely to Tam Glen, a poor man who has won her love.

Here is the poem in traditional Broad Scots, followed by a glossary to help you translate the dialect.

***

### **Tam Glen**
*by Robert Burns*

My heart is a-breaking, dear tittie! 
Some counsel unto me draw near; 
Gie a thought to the lassie that’s woefu’, 
A’ depressed wi’ the cahr o’ her gear. 

My minnie does constantly deave me, 
And preaches o’ siller an’ lairds; 
Whenever he comes down to see me, 
I thought I was promised to Laird’s.

There’s Lowrie, the laird o’ Dumeller, 
“Gude day to you, brute!” he comes ben; 
He murmurs and havers o’ siller, 
But ne’er a blithe look frae Tam Glen. 

There’s Sandy, the laird o’ the Moorland, 
Has doup o’ cash, houses, and land; 
But a lad that is true to his true love 
Is mair to my mind than them a’. 

My daddie cries, parritch and kail, 
And tells me I’m wrong to refuse; 
He says that a poor man is naething, 
And wealth is the thing I should choose.

But Tam has a twinkling blithe e’e, 
My heart leaps to hear his sweet voice; 
His cheek is as red as the rose, 
And Tam is the lad o’ my choice! 

Yestreen at the Valentine’s dealing, 
My heart to my mou gied a stend; 
For thrice I drew ane without failing, 
And thrice it was written—Tam Glen! 

The last Halloween I was waukin 
My droukit sark-sleeve, as ye ken; 
His likeness cam up the house stalkin, 
And the form o’ it Tammas Glen! 

Come counsel dear tittie, don’t tarry— 
I’ll gie you my bonnie black hen, 
If ye will advise me to marry 
The lad I lo’e dearly, Tam Glen!

***

### **Glossary of Scots Terms:**

*   **Tittie:** Sister, or very close female friend.
*   **Gear:** Possessions / financial state.
*   **Minnie:** Mother.
*   **Deave:** Deafen / annoy with constant nagging.
*   **Siller:** Silver / money.
*   **Laird:** A wealthy landowner.
*   **Ben:** Inside the house.
*   **Havers:** Speaks nonsense.
*   **Doup:** A heap or bottomless amount.
*   **Parritch and kail:** Oatmeal porridge and cabbage broth (symbolizing a life of basic, poor food).
*   **Blithe e’e:** Cheerful eye.
*   **Mou gied a stend:** Mouth gave a leap (her heart jumped into her throat).
*   **Waukin:** Washing/wetting (part of an old Folk ritual on Halloween to see a future husband's ghost).
*   **Droukit sark-sleeve:** Drenched shirt-sleeve.
*   **Lo’e:** Love.

### **The Story of the Poem:**
Meg's mother and father are desperate for her to marry for money ("siller"), pushing rich men like Lowrie and Sandy on her. However, Meg has used traditional Scots folk superstitions—drawing names on Valentine's Day and performing a Halloween wetting-of-the-sleeve ritual—and every time, fate points to **Tam Glen**. She ends the poem offering her prized possession (her "bonnie black hen") to her friend if her friend will just give her the advice she wants to hear: to follow her heart and marry Tam.
